Heavy rain will be the name of the game for the mid-week period 
across South Florida. By the time Wednesday rolls around, most 
guidance is in very good agreement that mid level troughing over the 
northern Gulf will continue to deepen and likely cut off from the 
rest of the jet stream. As mentioned in the previous discussion, 
eastward propagation of this feature has continued to trend slower 
among ensemble and deterministic model guidance, which is increasing 
confidence for more widespread heavy rainfall impacts. The main 
reason for this happening is due to a strengthening area of mid 
level high pressure centered over the Ohio River valley. As 
expansive ridging stretches north across the Mississippi River 
valley and into the Midwest, a Rex Block will begin to set up across 
the eastern CONUS, with a strong 587 dam H5 high parked over the 
Appalachians. The position and strength of this high will ultimately 
determine the track of the low pressure feature in the Gulf. A 
faster and more northern tracking system may keep the highest 
rainfall amounts further north of South Florida, while a slower and 
more southerly track will likely push rainfall amounts towards the 
higher end of the spectrum.

The synoptic pattern at the surface looks a little more messy and 
there is less confidence on how exactly certain features will play 
out. As is already being observed on mid-level water vapor imagery, 
deepening surface troughing along the Gulf, along with positive 
vorticity advection at the base of the mid-level shortwave, will 
help kick start an area of surface low pressure. This weak surface 
low will look to slide eastward and onto the Florida Gulf Coast by 
Wednesday morning. With surface high pressure still remaining quite 
strong over the mid-Atlantic coastal United States, pressure 
gradients across the region will continue to tighten as this low 
pressure feature begins to traverse across the state. As a result, 
breezy easterly conditions will continue to be common across South 
Florida (15 to 20 mph), with gusts up to 35 mph along the immediate 
Atlantic coast line. Some urban areas along the coasts of Palm Beach 
and Broward may see some frequent gusts of 30 mph, but the chances 
of sustained Wind Advisory conditions for Wednesday seem unlikely, 
with only about a 30% chance of reaching criteria. 

Several factors will aid the heavy rainfall threat for the Wednesday 
and Thursday period. More favorable convergence and ascent should be 
available as a stationary front slides southward across the 
peninsula. Precipitable water values (PWAT) will climb into the 1.8 
to 2 inch range late Wednesday, which is within the 90th percentile 
for this time of year. Additionally, as the mid-level shortwave 
feature continues to propagate east, winds aloft will increase out 
of the west. This will be exactly opposite to the mean wind flow at 
the surface, which will be out of the east. This set up of opposing 
wind patterns aloft and at the surface increases the potential for 
pinned storms along the coast. Frictional coastal convergence will 
continue to supply ascent and moisture along the shoreline, allowing 
new storms to continue to develop and begin training. The main 
concern with training and pinned storms is that several rounds of 
rain may fall over a specific area over the course of a few hours. 
As of now, there is large model spread between the worst case 
scenario amounts and the most likely rain amounts. Large swaths of 
the eastern metro area may see 2 to 4 inches through Thursday night. 
Locally heavier amounts of 6 to 8 inches will be more of a concern 
over Palm Beach county, where there is a 1 in 10 chance of this 
occurring. However, an isolated outlier of up to 10 to 12 inches 
cannot be ruled out. Model soundings depict a favorable set up for 
heavy rain, with long and skinny CAPE profiles up to 1000 J/kg. As a 
result, the Weather Prediction Center has outlined a Slight Risk of 
urban flash flooding for the Wednesday and Thursday period. Poor 
drainage locations and low lying areas will be at highest risk. 
Remember to never drive, walk, or wade through flooded roadways.

The forecast beyond Thursday still remains quite uncertain, but 
guidance is depicting several locations that may be favorable for 
the development of a new low pressure center along the Atlantic 
coast of South Florida. Overall, mid-level troughing over Florida 
will continue to favor unsettled weather as we head into the 
weekend. Some models show a new low developing further to the 
southeast and over the Bahamas, which may keep heavier rain away 
from South Florida. Other models depict the low riding up the 
Florida coast, which would keep the chances of rain fairly high.
